summary: Key takeaways Wallets on the official $TRUMP dinner leaderboard held about $9.1 million at the November 16 cutoff, against roughly $148 million for the first dinner in May 2025, a drop of close to 94% in visible dollar value. That does not mean 94% of investors withdrew cash: the token price fell sharply, and the two leaderboards are not identical in size or method. The top 10 wallets held about 81% of the tokens on the public board, and the top 29 about 95%. Public Citizen traced 66 of the 130 displayed wallets to exchanges that restrict US customers, which is not proof about who attended. Donald Trump’s latest meme coin dinner came with a striking financial comparison: wallets displayed on the official $TRUMP dinner leaderboard held approximately $9.1 million in tokens at the November 16 cutoff, compared with roughly $148 million associated with the first dinner in May 2025. That puts the decline in the publicly measured dollar value at close to 94%. It does not mean investors withdrew 94% of their cash, or that 94% fewer people turned up for dinner. Trump hosted the third event for major $TRUMP holders at his Virginia golf club on Sunday, November 22. The gathering itself was new, but the more interesting story is what the leaderboard reveals about a token that was once able to turn a private invitation into a market-wide buying contest. NewsBTC previously covered an earlier $TRUMP meme coin dinner rally. This time, the numbers tell a considerably less flattering story about the value attached to that privilege. What the 94% Figure Actually Measures The roughly $9.1 million estimate comes from Public Citizen’s November 22 review of the 130 wallets displayed on the final public leaderboard. Its researchers counted 9,794,832.87 $TRUMP tokens and valued them at approximately $0.93 each at the November 16, 9 a.m. Eastern cutoff. The older $148 million comparison refers to the first gala’s leaderboard in May 2025. # Name Wallet Time-weighted holdings Latest $TRUMP balance Days held 1 FastX Dd54…uHDD 1,389,617.57 1,771,794.76 39.45 2 few DNLo…EoY6 1,093,044.76 1,000,000.00 35.75 3 Unitas Mhgx…itas 997,566.73 1,241,671.11 46.33 4 taotao BWgb…drJH 984,339.81 1,147,626.05 40.20 5 Yulia Gzyw…d6cp 966,503.35 1,126,182.24 40.23 6 GoTrump 3MwE…R1oS 453,211.23 459,963.62 46.34 7 FASTXCO H1fu…hh1c 436,614.04 700,002.00 29.24 8 ymca 8TUd…kg3S 137,348.63 140,000.96 45.98 9 3Eye 8DHk…qRjW 117,063.01 200,000.00 27.43 10 cl16 FNUY…Mts9 118,840.61 122,552.25 45.45 Source: Official $TRUMP Gala Dinner Leaderboard (November 16, 2026). Rankings based on time-weighted token holdings. Wallet entries do not necessarily represent individual attendees. That works out to a decline of roughly 93.9%, rounded to 94%. But the events did not have identical leaderboard sizes or necessarily identical valuation methods. More importantly, the token’s price fell dramatically between the two events. A lower marked-to-market balance can reflect falling prices even if some holders retain comparable token quantities. Calling this a 94% collapse in new investment would therefore be wrong. The narrower conclusion is still hard to ignore: the value represented by the public competition for dinner access is a small fraction of what it was at the first event. The leaderboard also should not be mistaken for a headcount. While the public display showed 130 wallets, organizers said 185 wallets qualified under the event’s rules. One person can control multiple wallets, and a wallet can be held for an organization. Neither figure identifies exactly who attended Sunday night’s dinner. A Few Wallets Still Control Most of the Leaderboard The smaller overall value is only part of the picture. Public Citizen found that the top 10 wallets held about 81% of the tokens on the public board. The top 29 accounted for approximately 95%. Those top-ranked wallets were also eligible for a special VIP reception. The concentration matters because a leaderboard is marketed as a contest between investors, but its aggregate value can be dominated by a very small number of positions. Looking at the $9.1 million as if it represented broad, evenly distributed enthusiasm would be as misleading as treating all 130 wallet entries as separate people. There is a revealing detail near the bottom of Public Citizen’s review: the wallet ranked No. 130 held only 9.71 $TRUMP, worth about $9 at the snapshot. It qualified because the competition measured time-weighted holdings over the scoring period, rather than the balance left in the wallet at the very end. That is perfectly compatible with the rules. It also shows why a dinner ranking cannot be read as a simple list of fresh purchases or long-term conviction. There is another market point here. A buyer who wants dinner access can acquire the token and hedge some of the price risk elsewhere. Holding a spot position long enough to earn a place does not necessarily make someone a directional believer in the coin. In that sense, the competition measures an incentive to qualify, not a clean vote of confidence in future returns. The Wallet Trail Raises Questions, Not Conclusions About Guests Public Citizen’s researchers traced 66 of the 130 displayed wallets, or 51%, to direct transfers from exchanges that restrict US customers. Those wallets represented about 4.35 million $TRUMP, roughly 44% of the public board’s token holdings. Among the top 29 VIP-ranked wallets, 15 had received tokens directly from such exchanges, according to the group’s November 22 findings. That is useful on-chain information. It is not proof that 66 dinner guests were foreign nationals, that all those exchanges served prohibited customers, or that any particular attendee broke a rule. An exchange withdrawal identifies a source of tokens, not a passport or the identity of the person controlling the receiving wallet. Public Citizen put a basic transparency problem plainly: “The names of the invitees have not been disclosed.” That sentence matters because a wallet address, however transparent its transaction history, cannot supply the accountability that a named guest list would provide. The event’s official website states: “ GetTrumpMemes.com is not political and has nothing to do with any political campaign or any political office or governmental agency. GetTrumpMemes.com · Official website That is the organizers’ characterization. It does not remove the transparency question created when holders of a president-linked digital asset can compete for personal access to the president. Neither does that question, by itself, prove an improper exchange of favors. The Dinner Still Has Value. The Token’s Investment Case Is Another Matter. There is a credible bullish counterargument. An exclusive dinner is a limited, experience driven reward. Its value to attendees need not move in lockstep with the coin’s market capitalization, and falling token prices can make it cheaper for new participants to qualify. The gala went ahead, and its promoters continue to offer other experiences to holders. But that is precisely why we should be careful about treating an invitation contest as evidence of a durable investment base. Access is an incentive. It is not a claim on business earnings, and it does not put a floor under the price of the coin. The most uncomfortable part of this comparison for $TRUMP holders is not that the dinner was smaller or less glamorous. The available figures do not establish either claim. It is that the token’s most recognizable promotional feature remains personal access, while the dollar value visible on the public leaderboard has fallen dramatically since the first event. In our view, that weakens the argument that repeated celebrity events, by themselves, can sustain the market’s appetite for the token. A more persuasive sign of recovering demand would be durable, independently observable holdings beyond a contest period, with less dependence on a few top-ranked wallets. The next useful data would be post-event wallet balances and exchange flows, measured against the November 16 snapshot, not just another photograph from the dinner. For now, the 94% comparison is a warning about the dollar value of the visible leaderboard, not proof of a 94% investor exodus. That distinction makes the story more credible, and no less troubling for anyone relying on the dinner promotion as an investment thesis. content: Valuation data from the official $TRUMP meme coin dinner leaderboard reveals a nearly 94% drop in visible dollar value compared to the first gala in May 2025. While analysts note the decline partly reflects falling token prices rather than direct cash withdrawals, ownership remains heavily concentrated among a few top wallets. The event continues to highlight transparency questions regarding participant identities and exchange-funded wallets.

title: Fusionist ACE Bridge Exploit: $5.7M Loss Estimate, Bithumb Freezes Trading
summary: Key takeaways The Fusionist ACE bridge exploit is estimated at $5.7 million across two stages, according to SlowMist, which is not an audited final total. About $1.87 million in proceeds was traced to the attacker, while 53.7 million genuine ACE tokens, valued near $3.7 million, were reportedly withdrawn through the bridge. Bithumb halted ACE trading on November 23 after finding signs that abnormally issued ACE had entered exchanges. In the material reviewed, Fusionist has not published a reconciled loss figure or a technical post-mortem. The Fusionist ACE bridge exploit has produced an estimated $5.7 million in losses across two stages, according to SlowMist’s incident tracker. After unbacked ACE tokens were minted on BNB Chain and sold, traders reportedly used the resulting price collapse to withdraw real ACE from the project’s Endurance bridge reserves. The fallout reached centralized exchanges on Monday, November 23: Bithumb halted ACE trading after finding indications that abnormally issued tokens had entered crypto exchanges. This was not one attacker walking away with $5.7 million in a single transaction. The distinction matters. Roughly $1.87 million was traced through the attacker’s proceeds, while another 53.7 million genuine ACE tokens, valued around $3.7 million at the incident’s reference prices, were reportedly withdrawn through the bridge. SlowMist lists a combined $5.7 million loss estimate, not an audited final total. The bridge’s most basic promise, that a token issued on one chain corresponds to something real on another, is precisely what now needs proving. A Privileged Minter Printed Tokens That Had No Backing Security firm Blockaid flagged the Fusionist bridge-minter exploit on November 22. Its alert described the mechanism bluntly: “ A privileged token-bridge minter minted unbacked ACE and sold it for USDT. Blockaid · November 22 alert The firm initially estimated that about $1.04 million had been extracted while the attack was still ongoing. That was an interim snapshot, not a cap on the damage. Blockchain-monitoring account Onchain Lens subsequently reported that an attacker had routed 1,091.5 ETH, valued at about $1.87 million at the time, through Tornado Cash. That observation traces a movement of proceeds, not an extra $1.87 million to add on top of the initial extraction estimate. The values describe different points in the same suspected attacker’s fund flow. Fusionist acknowledged an apparent ongoing ACE exploit on BNB Smart Chain on Sunday and asked users to suspend transfers, trading and bridging on that network. It has not, in the material reviewed, provided a reconciled loss figure or a technical post-mortem identifying how the privileged minting authority was abused. A bridge minter is supposed to create a token representation only when the corresponding value is properly accounted for. Once the right to mint is misused, a chain can show perfectly ordinary-looking balances that have no matching backing. It is a familiar failure mode: NewsBTC previously covered a bridge-role exploit that minted unbacked tokens at CrediX. That earlier case does not establish Fusionist’s root cause, but it illustrates why elevated bridge permissions are such a consequential security boundary. Traders Found a Second Exit Through Real ACE Reserves The subsequent drain may prove more important than the initial minting spree. According to SlowMist’s November 22 incident entry, traders bought the sharply discounted ACE created by the market disruption and used the cross-chain bridge to withdraw about 53.7 million genuine ACE from the Endurance-side reserves. SlowMist valued that withdrawal at approximately $3.7 million. Here is the mechanism without the jargon. A representation of ACE on BNB Chain suddenly became cheap because unauthorized supply had flooded the market. A bridge that would still accept those tokens in exchange for ACE on Endurance offered an obvious difference in value. Anyone able to complete that conversion could receive real tokens in return for deeply discounted ones. The trading opportunity existed because the backing and the circulating representation were no longer in a trustworthy relationship. The $3.7 million figure is a valuation of the ACE reserve outflow, not proof that every recipient sold those tokens for $3.7 million in cash. Nor does it mean every trader involved helped compromise the minter. There is a meaningful difference between initiating the security breach and trading through a system whose defenses have already failed. Those distinctions should not obscure the core problem. A bridge can have technically valid transactions and still produce an economically disastrous result. If unbacked supply can be redeemed for genuine reserves, the checks have failed where they matter most. Bithumb’s Monday Halt Shows How Far the Problem Travelled Bithumb suspended ACE deposits and withdrawals early on November 23. It then halted trading effective 7:30 a.m. Korea time, according to its follow-up ACE security notice. The exchange said, in a translation from its Korean announcement, that it had: “ confirmed indications that abnormally issued ACE had entered cryptocurrency exchanges. Bithumb · ACE security notice It identified two related BNB Chain transactions and a second transaction. Those records are important evidence leads, but a full independent decoding of the transaction trail remains outstanding. Bithumb’s wording is careful: it reported signs of abnormal supply entering exchanges, not a finding that every ACE token in customer accounts is invalid. The trading suspension is a protective response, not a finalized determination of customer losses. Still, it creates a practical problem for holders who never used the bridge. If tokens are fungible within a market, exchanges and the issuer need a credible method for identifying affected supply and deciding how deposits, balances and trades will be treated. The Real Security Question Is Why the Bridge Could Honor the Claims There is an understandable temptation to focus on the enormous minting figures. The more consequential question is what happened when those tokens met the bridge’s reserves. A system does not need to lose control of its entire blockchain to suffer a serious failure in one privileged contract role. Nor should a successful-looking bridge transaction count as evidence that the asset being transferred was fully backed. Our assessment The response cannot end with a pause notice and a promise to investigate. Fusionist needs to show which minting permissions were affected, whether they have been revoked, how much ACE was created without backing, how the Endurance-side reserve changed and what claims remain outstanding. Exchanges need a defensible token-treatment plan, and holders need to know whether there is a shortfall and who is responsible for covering it. There is a fair counterargument: the $5.7 million figure is an external estimate, market prices moved during the incident, and the precise compromise method is not established. SlowMist categorizes the incident as private-key leakage, but that classification is not a substitute for an official technical finding. It would also be premature to treat a cautious exchange halt as proof that every affected customer suffered a loss. Those qualifications change how the numbers should be reported. They do not make the underlying bridge-accounting failure less serious. The next credible milestone is not a restored interface or a reassuring social post. It is a transparent reconciliation of the tokens minted, the reserves withdrawn and the assets still available to back legitimate ACE claims. Until that exists, the estimated $5.7 million fallout remains a warning about both token security and the risks of trusting a bridge’s accounting. content: The Fusionist ACE bridge suffered an exploit resulting in an estimated $5.7 million in losses across two stages, according to security firm SlowMist. The incident involved unbacked ACE tokens being minted on BNB Chain, followed by traders withdrawing genuine ACE from Endurance reserves. In response to abnormal supply entering exchanges, Bithumb halted ACE trading.
